slides.text: Git 3.0 is switching its default hash from SHA-1 to SHA-256. Scott Chacon, GitHub's co-founder, argues the change will cost the industry **years of broken tooling** for a security problem that barely applies to how real attacks happen.

SHA-1 counts as "broken" because researchers can manufacture two files with the same hash. Nobody has used that trick to sneak malicious code into a real project, though. The cheaper way in is still paying off a tired maintainer.

panel.small: cheaper than any hash collision, per Chacon

slides.text: Chacon's real argument: **trust in Git was never about the hash.** It comes from where you pull code from, an idea he traces back to Linus Torvalds at Git's founding. Real supply-chain attacks come from hijacked packages and compromised maintainers, not engineered collisions.

Not everyone bought it. One developer in the discussion pointed out that SHAttered was a working proof of concept in 2017, not theory, and that a collision alone can smuggle malicious code once two repos share a commit hash. **Chacon undersold the risk,** they argued.

The migration cost is real too. One developer who tried SHA-256 repos over a year ago found CI runners and actions simply broke. GitHub still doesn't support SHA-256 repositories at all, and **mixing both hash types in submodules** has no clean answer yet.

Others pushed back on "train wreck." Git's own migration docs say SHA-1 repos keep working untouched, only new repos default to SHA-256, and the two hash names map one to one. **One developer called it a friendly migration,** not a disaster.

My rule before adopting any "security upgrade": map the actual attack path first. One commenter guessed the real driver here is compliance, since **SHA-1 is banned outright under FIPS 140-2** at some organizations, not a working exploit anyone has run against Git.
Have you shipped a security migration that fixed a theoretical risk and broke real workflows for months? **Tell me what happened,** and save this for when Git 3.0 lands in your CI pipeline.
